docs.title: Voxima developer manual
docs.text:
Voxima makes educational videos from C++ code: vector graphics, math and text in any language, animation written as C++20 coroutines, text-to-speech narration, and subtitles in every language of the video.

You write the scenes in C++ and build them as a plugin; the voxima program you build loads it, and renders a video (or plays it in a window while you work). The words are in script files, one per language, so one set of scenes serves every language.

docs.text:

  2. Your first video: build, preview and render a small plugin.
  3. The examples: small plugins for each part of this manual.

docs.title: Animation and coroutines
docs.text:
A scene is a C++20 coroutine. It runs a little each frame and pauses at every co_await, so you write an animation as ordinary top-to-bottom code instead of a state machine:

Scene intro( Stage &stage, Script & )
{
    auto &title = stage.visuals.add( make_text( *stage.theme, "Hello", FontStyle{ Intent::TITLE } ) );
    co_await fade_in( stage, title, 0.5s );   // frames pass here
    co_await wait_for( stage, 1s );
    co_await fade_out( stage, title, 0.5s );
}

The code on this page is from the coroutines example (examples/coroutines), which is built with Voxima.

A Scene is the coroutine type (Scene is an alias of Coroutine). Everything you can co_await in one is a Scene too: the animation verbs, wait_for, narration, and other scenes.

docs.title: Waiting
docs.text:
co_await wait_for( stage, 1.5s );     // a pause
co_await wait_frames( 10 );           // exactly 10 frames, whatever the frame rate
co_await next_frame();                // one frame

docs.title: Doing things at the same time
docs.text:
choreograph runs several animations together and finishes when the last one does:

co_await choreograph(
    fade_in( stage, title, 0.5s ),
    grow_in( stage, circle, 0.8s ),
    wait_for( stage, 1s ) );              // (a narration.play() goes here, to run with them)

When the number of animations is only known at run time, collect them in a std::vector<Coroutine> and use choreograph_all:

std::vector<Coroutine> running;
for ( Visual *item: items )
    running.push_back( fade_in( stage, *item, 0.4s ) );
co_await choreograph_all( std::move( running ) );

To start things one after another with an overlap, use stagger (see Animation verbs).

docs.title: Running something every frame
docs.text:
For your own animations, tween calls a function once per frame with how far along it is, 0 to 1, shaped by an ease:

co_await tween( stage, 1.5s, ease_cubic_in_out, [&]( float t )
{
    circle.position = { -4.F + 8.F * t, 0.F };
} );

tween always makes at least two frames, a first (t = 0) and a last (t = 1, exactly).

To keep one thing tied to another for as long as you like, add an updater. It runs every frame, after the scene has done its step and before the picture is drawn:

auto tie = stage.updaters.add( [&] { label.position = dot.position + Point{ 0.F, 0.4F }; } );
co_await move_along( stage, dot, path, 2s );     // the label goes with the dot

The returned handle ends the updater when it is destroyed; call tie.release() to let it run to the end of the scene instead. Updaters are cleared when a scene starts. If you remove a visual an updater uses, end the updater first.

docs.title: Lifetimes
docs.text: An animation refers to the visual it works on, by reference. The visual must stay on the stage until the animation is over. In particular, do not clear() the stage or morph a visual away while an animation that uses it is still running in a choreograph.

docs.title: Frame rate and length
docs.text: Nothing in a scene depends on the frame rate: times are in seconds, rounded to the nearest whole frame. A time that is not a whole number of frames (half a second at 25 fps) is a frame more or less. The render's length is however long the scene takes, including the narration it waits for.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
A Voxima video is made of three things, kept apart on purpose:

What it is Where it lives Scenes C++ coroutines that decide what is drawn and when A plugin you build (.so / .dll) Script The words: what is shown and what is narrated, in each language <lang>.huml files Theme The fonts and colors A built-in theme, or a .huml theme file

The voxima program has no scenes of its own. You give it a plugin (--plugin), a directory of scripts (--script-dir), the languages (--lang) and a theme, and it renders the scene called movie (or the ones you name with --scene) to a video with narration and subtitles, or plays it in a window (--preview).

                          voxima --plugin hello --script-dir scripts --lang en --lang fr
                                         |
   hello.so (scenes) ───────────────────►|◄─────────────── scripts/en.huml, fr.huml (words)
                                         |◄─────────────── theme (fonts, colors)
                                         ▼
                      final.mkv   (video + one audio and one subtitle track per language)

Keeping the words out of the C++ means one scene serves every language, and a writer can change the narration without recompiling anything.

docs.title: The stage
docs.text:
A scene draws on a Stage. Its parts:

  • stage.visuals: the group of everything that is drawn. You add visuals to it.
  • stage.theme: the fonts and the palette (stage.theme->palette().blue).
  • stage.camera: what part of the stage is seen (and the picture's size and frame rate).
  • stage.audio: the sound: narration, music and effects.
  • stage.updaters: small functions run every frame, to keep one thing tied to another.

Coordinates. The stage is measured in stage units, with y pointing up and the origin at the center of the picture. At the default zoom the picture is 16 units wide; at 16:9 that is 9 units tall, so the visible area runs about from -8 to 8 across and -4.5 to 4.5 up. Resolution does not matter to a scene: --width 1920 makes the same picture sharper, not bigger. Everything is vector graphics until the last moment.

Time. Durations are written with units (0.5s, 250ms) and turned into whole frames at the render's frame rate. A bare number does not compile, so a scene never has to guess between seconds and frames.

Color. A Color is red, green, blue and alpha, each 0 to 1. Pure white means "the theme's text color", so a scene written for a dark background stays readable on a light one. For anything that should suit any palette, use the palette's accents (red orange yellow green cyan blue purple pink, plus muted) instead of fixed colors. See Themes.

docs.title: Visuals
docs.text:
Everything drawn is a Visual: a position, a rotation, a scale, a color, an outline. Shapes (Circle, Rectangle, Line), laid-out text, formulas, charts and diagrams are all visuals, and most are a Group holding other visuals (a piece of text is a group of lines of words of glyphs). Add one to the stage with stage.visuals.add( ... ), which gives you back a reference to keep for animating it.

Two rules to remember:

  • A visual stays alive as long as it is in a group. The reference add returns is valid until you remove or clear the visual.
  • A scene starts on an empty stage, so it looks the same on its own as inside a movie.

docs.title: Scenes and movies
docs.text: A scene is a coroutine that animates the stage: Scene f( Stage &, Script & ) (Scene is just Coroutine). Scenes are registered by name, so any one of them can be rendered on its own, and a movie is a scene that plays other scenes.

docs.title: Registering a scene
docs.text:
Put one line next to the scene (core/SceneRegistry.h):

Scene show_intro( Stage &stage, Script &script )
{
    // build visuals on stage.visuals, co_await animations, narration, other scenes ...
}
REGISTER_SCENE( "intro", "The title and the first formula", show_intro );

The function, or any callable, only has to convert to a Director (std::function<Coroutine( Stage &, Script & )>); a scene that needs more arguments is wrapped in a lambda. There is no list to edit: adding a scene is writing it and adding that line.

docs.title: A movie
docs.text:
A movie is an ordinary scene whose body plays others:

Scene movie( Stage &stage, Script &script )
{
    co_await sequence( stage, script, { "intro", "morphs", "outro" } );
}
REGISTER_SCENE( "movie", "The whole thing", movie );
  • play( stage, script, "name" ) plays one registered scene and finishes when it does.
  • sequence( stage, script, { ... } ) plays several, one after another.
  • Scenes can also run at the same time: co_await choreograph( play( ... ), play( ... ) ). (Each play clears the stage first, so do that only for scenes that share nothing.)

The stage is cleared before each scene (PlayOptions::clear_stage, on by default), so a scene looks the same on its own as in a movie and never depends on what the one before left behind. Pass PlayOptions{ .clear_stage = false } for a scene that carries on from the previous one. The last scene's visuals stay on the stage.

docs.title: Choosing what to render
docs.text:
voxima --plugin build/myvideo --list-scenes   # the registered scenes and what they do (see Plugins)
voxima ...                                  # renders the scene called "movie"
voxima ... --scene morph-text               # one scene
voxima ... --scene morph-shapes --scene karaoke   # several, in the order given (a movie made on the spot)

An unknown name is reported (with the list) before any model or font is loaded, and exits with status 1. If no scene is called "movie" and there is no --scene, the only registered scene is used; with several and no "movie", the list is shown as an error.

docs.title: Plugins: scenes outside the program
docs.text:
voxima itself has no scenes: they are in plugins, shared libraries (a .dll, or a .so) loaded with --plugin (repeatable; the extension may be left out). A plugin is its scenes, registered as above, and one line in one of its files (core/Plugin.h):

VOXIMA_PLUGIN();

voxima --plugin build/myvideo --list-scenes
voxima --plugin build/myvideo ... --scene karaoke

In CMake a plugin is voxima_add_plugin( name sources... ) (see Your own plugin project).

A plugin shares the program's strings, functions and coroutines, so it must be built just as the program was: the same compiler and version, standard library, and Debug or Release, against the same Voxima. Each says what it was built with, and one that does not match is refused when it is loaded, naming both, rather than crashing.

With --preview, a rebuilt plugin is loaded again by itself: the scenes start again with the new code, and the window goes back to where it was in the scene being watched. F5 does the same, and loads the script again too. If the new build cannot be loaded, or a scene fails, it is shown in the window's title (and on stderr), and the next build is tried when it comes. (What is loaded is a copy, in the temporary directory, so the build can write over the file.)

See Installing and Your own plugin project for building Voxima and building a plugin against it.

Languages and narration are in Narration; missing glyphs in Rendering.

docs.title: The script
docs.text:
The script holds the words of a video, one file per language, apart from the scenes that show them. A scene asks the script for text; the script has it in every language. Adding a language means adding a file, not changing C++.

Script files are written in HUML, a plain, indentation-based data format.

docs.title: A script file
docs.text:
scripts/en.huml:

meta::
  lang: "en"
  inherit: null

voices::
  narrator: "chatterbox/en-voice-zero-robert-middleton.wav"

labels::
  title: "Voxima"
  chapter-1: "Building the project"

intro: """
  A script becomes a video.
  Vector shapes<,> animated with coroutines.
  Narrated and subtitled as it plays.
"""

steps::
  - "make config"
  - "make"
  • key:: starts a section; key: value is a value; - item is a list item; # starts a comment.
  • """ ... """ is a multi-line text: one entry per line. Line breaks matter: they are the points narration and subtitles are timed to (see Narration).
  • meta says which language the file is, and what it builds on (inherit, below).
  • voices names the narrators (see Narration).
  • labels is the usual place for short on-screen text: titles, captions, names.
  • Everything else is yours: name sections and keys as you like.

docs.title: Reading it from a scene
docs.text:
const std::string lang = script.master_language();

// a short label, with a fallback if it is missing
std::string title = script.label( lang, "title" );

// any value, by its path of keys
const huml::Value &steps = script.fetch( lang, "steps" );
for ( const auto &item: steps.as_list() )
    std::string step{ item.as_string() };

const auto &lines = script.fetch( lang, "intro" ).as_multiline();  // the lines of a multi-line text

A huml::Value is a string, number (as_int, as_double), as_bool, list (as_list), dict (as_dict) or multi-line text; is_string(), is_list() and so on tell which. master_language() is the first language given with --lang: what on-screen text is shown in. (When one video holds several languages, the others are heard and subtitled; see Languages.)

A key that is not there never fails quietly. fetch gives a missing value, and text made from it shows as a magenta box with a code in it, and is listed when the render ends (see Missing glyphs). script.label( lang, key, fallback ) takes a fallback for the text instead.

docs.title: Languages and regions
docs.text:
--lang en loads en.huml from the script directory. For a region, --lang fr-CA loads fr-CA.huml, or fr.huml if there is no such file; the language is still called fr-CA, so its subtitle track and metadata say so.

A file can build on another, so a region only has to say what differs:

# fr-CA.huml
meta::
  lang: "fr-CA"
  inherit: "fr"

labels::
  title: "Une vidéo en québécois"

inherit names another file (without .huml); the two are merged, section by section, with the inheriting file winning. So every key has a value, and regional overrides stay small. Use inherit: null for a file that builds on nothing.

docs.title: Markers: cue points in narration
docs.text:
Write a marker, {name}, in the narrated text where something should happen, in every language:

intro: """
  These show {a}various ease{b} animations.
"""

# fr.huml
intro: """
  Ceux-ci montrent {a}diverses animations{b} de lissage.
"""

Markers are never spoken or shown. Each language's narration gets a time for each, so a scene can say "until a" or "from a to b" and follow the speech in any language, where a word number would not carry over (words differ in number and length between languages). A name is letters, digits, _ and -. A literal brace is a doubled one: {{a}}.

docs.title: Written and spoken text
docs.text:
Text on screen is not always what should be said. In narrated text, <written|spoken> shows one and says the other:

The source lives in <src|source>, and we built <C++|see plus plus> in a weekend.
  • <written|spoken>: shows written, says spoken.
  • <written> (no bar): shows written and says nothing: a gap in the narration, for on-screen text with nothing to say out loud.
  • Subtitles use the written text.
  • <<, >> and || are a literal <, > and |. A < with no > after it is ordinary text ("a < b").

The Vector shapes<,> in the first listing is this form: the comma is shown in the subtitle but is not part of what is said.

docs.title: The examples
docs.text:
Voxima comes with example plugins, one folder each in examples/ (<prefix>/share/voxima/examples/ once installed). Each is a small project of its own: copy a folder out and change it. They are also what the code in this manual is taken from, and they are built with Voxima, so they keep working.

Example Shows Guide hello One scene: a title and a circle (the only scene of its plugin, so it plays by default) Your first video coroutines Waiting, doing things together, a change every frame, an updater Animation and coroutines layout Shapes, groups, placement, panels, lists, tables, tags Visuals and layout text-math Text, styled and right-to-left text, formulas, code, missing glyphs Text and math animation The animation verbs, connectors that follow, the camera Animation verbs and the camera morphing Shapes, letters, formulas, sentences and strokes that morph Morphing charts Plots, scatter plots, bar charts, diagrams, geometry Charts and diagrams narration Speech in several languages; words, lines and markers followed Narration and languages sound A sound made in code, and music Music and sound effects tour A movie scene that plays the other examples' scenes one after another Scenes and movies

docs.title: Running them
docs.text:
Built inside Voxima, every example goes to build/Release/plugins, a folder with nothing else in it, so they can all be loaded at once:

build/Release/voxima --plugin-dir build/Release/plugins --list-scenes

lists every scene of every example. Pick one with --scene, and give it a script folder (each example has a scripts/ folder with the words it needs; the narration scenes need the speech models):

build/Release/voxima --plugin-dir build/Release/plugins --script-dir examples/layout/scripts --lang en \
    --scene layout-basics --preview

Scene names are unique across the examples (layout-basics, morph-shapes), so they can be loaded together.

docs.title: The whole tour
docs.text:
The tour example has a movie scene that plays the scenes of the others one after another, which is what renders when you give no --scene. Load everything and give it its own script folder:

build/Release/voxima --plugin-dir build/Release/plugins --script-dir examples/tour/scripts --lang en \
    --theme "Academic Classic" --preview

Music is optional: set VOXIMA_MUSIC to a sound file for some under it. The narrated scenes are left out, since they need the speech models; render them on their own with --scene (see the narration example). Some themes' fonts lack a few math symbols, which show as magenta boxes and are listed at the end of the render.

docs.title: Your first video
docs.text: This builds the small example plugin that comes with Voxima, previews it in a window, and renders it to a video file. You need Voxima built and installed and the fonts.

docs.title: 1. Copy the example
docs.text:
cp -r <prefix>/share/voxima/examples/hello my-video
cd my-video

It holds three files:

  • hello.cpp: one scene, written in C++.
  • scripts/en.huml: the words, for English (a title, here).
  • CMakeLists.txt: builds hello.cpp into a plugin.

docs.title: 2. Look at the scene
docs.text:
// A plugin of scenes: build it (see CMakeLists.txt), then
//
//     voxima --plugin build/hello --script-dir scripts --lang en --theme "Academic Classic" --preview
//
// With --preview, rebuilding it while the window is open plays the scene again with the change.

#include <core/Animate.h>
#include <core/Plugin.h>
#include <core/SceneRegistry.h>
#include <core/Script.h>
#include <core/Stage.h>
#include <core/Wait.h>
#include <visuals/Circle.h>
#include <visuals/CreateText.h>
#include <visuals/Placement.h>

#include <memory>
#include <string>

using namespace std::chrono_literals;

VOXIMA_PLUGIN();

namespace
{
Scene hello( Stage &stage, Script &script )
{
    Theme &theme = *stage.theme;
    const std::string title{ script.fetch( script.master_language(), "title" ).as_string() };

    auto &words = stage.visuals.add( make_text( theme, title, FontStyle{ Intent::TITLE }.large() ) );
    move_to( words, { 0.F, 1.5F } );

    auto circle = std::make_unique<Circle>();
    circle->radius = 1.F;
    circle->color = theme.palette().blue;
    auto &dot = stage.visuals.add( std::move( circle ) );
    dot.position = { 0.F, -1.5F };

    co_await fade_in( stage, words, 0.8s );
    co_await grow_in( stage, dot, 0.6s );
    co_await indicate( stage, dot );
    co_await wait_for( stage, 1s );
}
}

// With one scene registered, it is what plays without --scene (several plugins together: name it with --scene)
REGISTER_SCENE( "hello", "A title and a circle", hello );

Read it top to bottom:

  • VOXIMA_PLUGIN(); marks the file as a plugin. It says which compiler and library it was built with, so voxima can refuse a mismatch.
  • hello is a scene: a coroutine that receives the Stage (what is drawn) and the Script (the words).
  • The text and the circle are visuals, added to stage.visuals. Then fade_in and grow_in bring them in from nothing.
  • co_await plays an animation and continues when it is over. Each line takes the time it names.
  • REGISTER_SCENE( "hello", ... ) gives the scene a name. With only one scene registered, that is what plays when you do not ask for another.

docs.title: 3. Build the plugin
docs.text:
Plugins are built with CMake, against the installed Voxima:

cmake -S . -B build -G Ninja -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release -DCMAKE_PREFIX_PATH=<prefix>
cmake --build build

The build type, the compiler and the standard library must be those Voxima was built with, which they are if you use the same compiler; see Your own plugin project.

You now have build/hello.so (build\hello.dll on Windows; it is .so on macOS too, not .dylib).

docs.title: 4. Preview it
docs.text:
<prefix>/bin/voxima --plugin build/hello --script-dir scripts --lang en \
    --theme "Academic Classic" --preview

A window opens and plays the scene. Leave it open, edit hello.cpp (change a color, a time, the circle's size), and rebuild: the scene starts again with your change, on its own. (F5 reloads the script too, so you can change the words just as quickly.) Space pauses; Esc closes the window.

docs.title: 5. Render it
docs.text:
<prefix>/bin/voxima --plugin build/hello --script-dir scripts --lang en \
    --theme "Academic Classic" --render-dir render

The video is render/final.mkv. Choose the format with --container (mp4, mkv, webm), --vcodec and --acodec, and the size with --width, --height and --fps. Rendering lists what is left in the render directory.
