docs.title: Installing
docs.text:
Voxima is distributed as source code. You build it once, then build your own scenes against that build. (A Conan package is planned, so that this step becomes a single command.)

Building from source is also what keeps your scenes working: the scenes you write are compiled into a plugin that the voxima program loads, and a plugin has to be built with the same compiler (and version), standard library, Debug or Release configuration, and Voxima version as the program. If you build both yourself, with one compiler, they match. A plugin that does not match is refused when it loads, with a message naming both builds, rather than crashing.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
A C++20 compiler GCC 14 or newer on Linux; MSVC 19.4 or newer on Windows; Apple clang on macOS (21 is known to work) CMake 3.31 or newer Ninja The build uses it Conan Version 2. It downloads and builds the libraries Voxima uses (pip install conan) Python 3 For Conan and for downloading the fonts git To get the source ffmpeg Voxima encodes and joins video, audio and subtitles by running ffmpeg, so it has to be on your PATH. Check with ffmpeg -version

Conan needs a default profile for your compiler once: conan profile detect. Voxima's code is C++20; set compiler.cppstd=20 in the profile (~/.conan2/profiles/default).

docs.title: Get the source
docs.text:
git clone git@github.com:iangodin/voxima.git
cd voxima

or download the source archive of a release from the project's GitHub page and unpack it. The clone includes the speech engine (extern/audio.cpp) and the reference voices (voices/).

docs.title: Build it
docs.text:
make config
make

make config runs Conan to get the libraries (the first time this builds several of them, which takes a while) and configures the Debug and Release builds. make builds the Release build. Then

build/Release/voxima --help

prints every option. These are the other targets:

Command What it does make debug Builds the Debug build, in build/Debug make test Builds Debug and runs the tests make install PREFIX=<dir> Installs the Release build: the program, the core library, the headers and the CMake package make clean Deletes build/ (run make config again afterwards)

Run voxima from the folder of the checkout, where it finds assets/fonts, models and voices. From anywhere else it looks for them as described under Fonts and Speech models and voices, or you can give them with options (--font-dir, --tts-model, --aligner-model, --tts-voice-dir).

docs.title: Install it (to build plugins elsewhere)
docs.text:
Plugins of your own can be built inside the checkout, or in a project of their own that finds Voxima through CMake. For the second, install the build somewhere:

make install PREFIX=$HOME/voxima-install

The rest of this manual calls that folder <prefix>. It holds

Where What <prefix>/bin/voxima The program: renders and previews videos <prefix>/lib/ The core library (libvoxima_core) and the speech engine library the program loads <prefix>/include/voxima/ The headers your scenes are written against <prefix>/lib/cmake/Voxima/ The CMake package, for find_package( Voxima ) <prefix>/share/voxima/examples/ Example plugin projects to start from, one folder each <prefix>/share/voxima/voices/ The reference voices for narration, with their sources and licenses <prefix>/share/voxima/download_fonts.py, download_models.py The scripts that download the fonts and the speech models <prefix>/share/doc/Voxima/ The manual (as a web site, open manual/index.html) and the licenses

Your own plugin project shows how to build against it.

docs.title: Fonts
docs.text:
The fonts are large and are not in the repository. Download them once, from the checkout:

python3 download_fonts.py

They go to assets/fonts, or to a directory you give the script (--help lists its options, and --list names the fonts without downloading anything). Voxima looks for fonts in the directory given with --font-dir, then in assets/fonts (relative to where you run it), then in $VOXIMA_FONTS, then in <prefix>/share/voxima/fonts (you can give the script that directory, to share the fonts between projects). Without the fonts, text cannot be drawn.

docs.title: Speech models and voices (only for narration)
docs.text:
Narration is made by a local text-to-speech model, which runs on your own machine: nothing is sent anywhere. The reference voices are in the repository, in voices/, and are installed with Voxima. The models are large (3.2 GB together) and are not; download them from the checkout:

python3 download_models.py

They go to models/ (which git does not track), in the folders Voxima expects. Run from an install (<prefix>/share/voxima/download_models.py), the script puts them in <prefix>/share/voxima/models instead, for every project to share; or give it a directory. It skips files you already have and resumes an interrupted download. --all also fetches the larger F16 versions, and --list says what it would fetch and where, without downloading anything. They are Q8_0 GGUF conversions in the Hugging Face repository audio-cpp/audio.cpp-gguf, under the licenses of the original models (Chatterbox: MIT; Qwen3-ForcedAligner: Apache-2.0):

File Used for Path in the models folder Option chatterbox-q8_0.gguf Speech Chatterbox-GGUF/chatterbox-q8_0.gguf --tts-model qwen3-forced-aligner-0.6b-q8_0.gguf Timing of the subtitles to the words (optional) Qwen3-ForcedAligner-0.6B-GGUF/qwen3-forced-aligner-0.6b-q8_0.gguf --aligner-model

Without its option, each model is looked for in models (relative to where you run voxima), then in $VOXIMA_MODELS, then in <prefix>/share/voxima/models, and the first folder that has the file is used. To download them yourself, take the two files from that repository (Chatterbox-GGUF/ and Qwen3-ForcedAligner-0.6B-GGUF/) and put them at those paths in one of these folders.

Each narrator speaks in the voice of a short reference clip (a few seconds of a real voice), named in your script's voices section. The clips are looked for under --tts-voice-dir; without it, under the first of voices (relative to where you run voxima), $VOXIMA_VOICES and <prefix>/share/voxima/voices that there is. See Narration; the clips that come with Voxima, and their licenses, are listed there too. A video with no narration needs none of these.

You can use a GPU for the speech with --tts-backend cuda (the default, best, picks one that works), if CUDA was found when Voxima was configured. With cpu, --tts-threads sets how many threads it uses.

Go on to Your first video.

docs.title: Animation verbs and the camera
docs.text:
These are the common things to do to a visual. Each is a scene you co_await (or run several at once with choreograph). The code on this page is from the animation example (examples/animation), which is built with Voxima. Each takes the visual as it is now as its resting state and leaves it there, except the ones that take it away. All take a length in seconds and, where it makes sense, an ease.

co_await choreograph( fade_in( stage, *a, 0.5s ), slide_in( stage, *b, { 0.F, -3.F }, 0.8s ), grow_in( stage, *c, 0.6s ), fade_in( stage, ab, 0.8s ), fade_in( stage, bc, 0.8s ) );
co_await wait_for( stage, 0.3s );
co_await indicate( stage, *b );
co_await move_by( stage, *b, { 0.F, 2.5F }, 0.8s, ease_cubic_in_out ); // the connectors bend with it
co_await move_by( stage, *b, { 0.F, -2.5F }, 0.8s, ease_cubic_in_out );
co_await wait_for( stage, 0.3s );
co_await choreograph( fade_out( stage, *a, 0.5s ), slide_out( stage, *b, { 0.F, 3.F }, 0.8s ), shrink_out( stage, *c, 0.6s ), fade_out( stage, ab, 0.5s ), fade_out( stage, bc, 0.5s ) );
Verb Does fade_in, fade_out From nothing to how it is, and back (it is left there, invisible: remove it if it should go) fade_to( stage, v, opacity ) To an opacity, and it stays there: dim with 0.3F, bring back with 1.F (Visual::opacity) grow_in, shrink_out Grow from its own center, fading in; the reverse grow_from_edge( stage, v, Anchor::BOTTOM, ...) Grow from one edge, which stays where it is: a bar of a chart, a gauge slide_in( stage, v, offset, ...), slide_out Come in from offset away (stage units), fading in; go out to it move_by( stage, v, offset, ...) Move by an offset move_along( stage, v, path, ... , turn ) Follow a Path; with turn, face the way it is going turn_about( stage, v, center, degrees, ...) Go round a point, turning with it indicate( stage, v, factor, ...) Swell by factor (1.2) and back draw_on( stage, v, duration ) Trace the outlines with a line, then fade the fill in: for text, shapes and paths circumscribe, flash Draw a line round a visual with a pen; a ring that spreads from its edge. Options: PointOutOptions stagger( stage, visuals, delay, verb ) Run a verb on each of several visuals, each starting delay after the last

stagger takes the verb as a function from a visual to a Scene, and children_of( group ) lists a group's direct children:

co_await stagger( stage, children_of( row ), 0.12s, [&]( Visual &v ) { return slide_in( stage, v, { 0.F, 1.5F }, 0.5s ); } );

draw_on, circumscribe and flash draw their outlines in the group the visual is a child of (give it as the last argument if that is not the stage), so the visual has to be a direct child of that group.

docs.title: Easing
docs.text:
An ease turns how far along something is, t from 0 to 1, into how far along it looks: slow at first, overshooting, bouncing. It is a plain function of t, so any moment can be worked out in any order.

Ease Feel ease_linear Steady ease_cubic_in, ease_cubic_out, ease_cubic_in_out Smooth: slow start, slow end, or both ease_back_in, ease_back_out, ease_back_in_out Pull back first, or overshoot a little ease_elastic_in, ease_elastic_out, ease_elastic_in_out Spring ease_there_and_back, ease_there_and_back_with_pause( pause ) Out to 1 and back to 0, for a pulse; with a stay at 1 for that part of the time. Include core/EaseThereAndBack.h

Pass one to a verb or to tween. Any function from float to float works (EaseFunction is std::function<float( float )>), so writing your own is one line:

auto smooth = []( float t ) { return t * t * ( 3.F - 2.F * t ); };

The back and elastic eases are also types, with parameters for how far and how quick the swings are (see core/EaseBack.h, core/EaseElastic.h).

docs.title: Tying things together
docs.text:
A label that follows a moving thing, a line between two moving boxes: use updaters (stage.updaters.add). A Connector has a ready-made one, follow:

auto &ab = stage.visuals.add( make_connector( *a, *b, { .gap = 0.1F } ) );
auto &bc = stage.visuals.add( make_connector( *b, *c, { .gap = 0.1F } ) );
auto tie_ab = follow( stage, ab );
auto tie_bc = follow( stage, bc );

docs.title: The camera
docs.text:
stage.camera says what part of the stage is seen: its center (a point, stage units) and zoom (1 is the whole 16-unit-wide picture; 2 shows half of that, so things look twice as big, lines included).

const Point peak = axes.at( pi / 2, 1.0 );
co_await camera_to( stage, { peak, 3.F }, 1.5s );
co_await wait_for( stage, 1s );
co_await camera_to( stage, { axes.at( 3 * pi / 2, -1.0 ), 3.F }, 2s ); // then the trough after it
co_await wait_for( stage, 1s );
co_await camera_to( stage, { { 0.F, 0.F }, 1.F }, 1.5s );

camera_frame( stage, some_visual, 1s ) fits a visual (or an AABB) to the picture instead. The zoom moves evenly in its logarithm and the center follows, so zooming in on something looks like moving in on it. camera_to and camera_frame default to ease_cubic_in_out. view_framing( camera, box, margin ) works out the view that fits a box, if you want to use it yourself.

The camera is at its default at the start of every scene.

docs.title: Charts and diagrams
docs.text: The code on this page is from the charts example (examples/charts), which is built with Voxima.

docs.title: Axes and graphs
docs.text:
AxesOptions options;
options.placement = placement;
options.x = { -6.0, 6.0 };
options.y = { -2.5, 2.5 };
options.width = 12.F;
options.height = 5.F;
options.grid = true;
auto &axes = stage.visuals.add( make_axes( *stage.theme, options ) );
co_await draw_axes( stage, axes, 2.5s );

Other options: x_label, y_label, numbers, arrows, grid_x, grid_y, custom x_tick_labels / y_tick_labels (a tick with its own text: a year, "π"), and colors and thicknesses.

Add graphs of functions with plot, and draw them on:

auto &wave = axes.add_plot( plot( axes, []( double x ) { return std::sin( x ); }, { .name = "sin x" } ) );
co_await draw( stage, wave, 2s );

GraphOptions orange;
orange.color = stage.theme->palette().orange;
orange.name = "1 / x";
auto &inverse = axes.add_plot( plot( axes, []( double x ) { return 1.0 / x; }, orange ) );
co_await draw( stage, inverse, 2s );

A function that blows up (like 1/x) is drawn in pieces on either side of the break. GraphOptions also sets the x range to plot, the number of samples, and the thickness. Each new graph takes the next color of the palette's series (blue, orange, green, purple, ...) unless you give one.

axes.at( x, y ) converts a point of the graph to a stage point: put things on the graph, or aim the camera at a peak with it.

A graph's curve can be dashed with GraphOptions::dash (see Dashed lines).

docs.title: Scatter plots
docs.text:
auto &measured = plot_axes.add_plot( scatter( plot_axes, { { 1, 1.5 }, { 2, 2.4 }, { 3.5, 3.0 }, { 5, 5.2 }, { 6.5, 5.6 }, { 8, 7.1 }, { 9.5, 7.4 } }, { .line = JoinStyle::SMOOTH, .name = "measured" } ) );
auto &noisy = plot_axes.add_plot( scatter( plot_axes, { { 1, 3.0 }, { 2.5, 2.2 }, { 4, 4.6 }, { 5.5, 3.1 }, { 7, 4.4 }, { 9, 5.0 } }, { .marker = MarkerShape::CROSS, .size = 0.14F, .name = "noisy" } ) );

marker is CIRCLE, SQUARE, DIAMOND, TRIANGLE, CROSS or PLUS; line joins the points: NONE, STRAIGHT or SMOOTH (a curve through them, which can overshoot between points far apart).

docs.title: Bar charts
docs.text:
auto &bars = stage.visuals.add( make_bar_chart( theme, {
    .categories = { "Q1", "Q2", "Q3", "Q4" },
    .series = { { "north", { 12, 19, 15, 22 } }, { "south", { 9, 14, 20, 17 } } },
    .width = 4.8F, .height = 4.F, .values = Range{ 0, 30 }, .value_labels = true } ) );
bars.position = { 4.9F, 0.6F };
add_legend( bars.axes(), make_legend( theme, legend_entries( bars ), { .horizontal = true } ), Anchor::TOP_LEFT );

Grouped by default; .stacked = true stacks them, .horizontal = true turns the chart on its side, .color_by_category = true gives each category its own color (for a single series), and negative values go below the axis. .value_labels writes the numbers on the bars.

docs.title: Legends
docs.text:
auto &key = add_legend( axes, make_legend( *stage.theme, { legend_entry( wave ), legend_entry( inverse ) } ), Anchor::TOP_RIGHT );

Name your plots and series (.name = ...): the legend takes names and colors from them.

docs.title: Number lines
docs.text:
auto &numbers = stage.visuals.add( make_number_line( theme, { .range = { 0.0, 10.0 }, .length = 7.F } ) );
numbers.position = { 3.8F, 1.4F };
numbers.add_interval( theme, 6.0, 9.0, palette.blue, { .closed_to = false } );
numbers.add_mark( theme, 2.5, "x", palette.orange );

docs.title: Diagrams
docs.text:
A Diagram is a set of labeled boxes (nodes) joined by arrows (edges), laid out in layers for you:

auto &flow = stage.visuals.add( make_diagram() );
flow.add_text_node( theme, "read", "Read input", label, {}, tinted( palette.blue ) );
flow.add_text_node( theme, "parse", "Parse", label, {}, tinted( palette.green ) );
flow.add_text_node( theme, "check", "Validate", label, {}, tinted( palette.green ) );
flow.add_text_node( theme, "run", "Run", label, {}, tinted( palette.orange ) );
flow.add_text_node( theme, "log", "Write a log", label, {}, tinted( palette.purple ) );
flow.add_edge( "read", "parse" );
flow.add_edge( "read", "check" );
flow.add_edge( "parse", "run" );
flow.add_edge( "check", "run" );
flow.add_edge( "run", "log" );
flow.layout_layers( { .layer_gap = 0.9F } );

Nodes are panels (flow.node( "run" )); give add_text_node a PanelOptions to tint one. add_node takes any visual as the content. Edges are connectors: flow.edge( i ), flow.edge_count(). If you move a node, call flow.update() (or tie it with follow( stage, flow )) and the arrows follow.

Build a diagram up on screen by staggering nodes then edges:

co_await stagger( stage, nodes, 0.25s, [&]( Visual &node ) { return grow_in( stage, node, 0.5s ); } );

docs.title: Connectors, callouts and braces
docs.text:
auto &ab = stage.visuals.add( make_connector( *a, *b, { .gap = 0.1F } ) );
auto &bc = stage.visuals.add( make_connector( *b, *c, { .gap = 0.1F } ) );
auto tie_ab = follow( stage, ab );
auto tie_bc = follow( stage, bc );
auto &note = stage.visuals.add( make_callout(
    make_paragraph( theme, "Both checks must finish before anything runs", label, 3.6F ),
    flow.node( "run" ) ) );
next_to( note.panel(), flow.node( "run" ), Anchor::RIGHT, 1.6F );
note.update();
stage.visuals.add( make_labeled_brace_beside( theme, list, Anchor::LEFT, "3 ideas", label, 0.25F, { .color = palette.muted } ) );

A callout is a panel with a pointer to a target; after moving either, call note.update(). Braces come in plain (make_brace( from, to ), make_brace_beside( visual, side )) and labeled forms.

A connector's line can be dashed with ConnectorOptions::dash (see Dashed lines).

docs.title: Arrows
docs.text:
A connector joins two visuals. For an arrow between points, or along a curve, use make_arrow, which takes the same options (but for gap) and stays where it is put. draw plays it on, the line and then the head:

auto &straight = stage.visuals.add( make_arrow( { -5.F, -1.F }, { -1.F, 1.F }, { .color = palette.blue } ) );
auto &curved = stage.visuals.add( make_arrow( *make_arc( { 3.F, -1.F }, 2.F, 180.F, 0.F ), { .arrow_at_start = true, .color = palette.orange } ) );
curved.set_drawn( 0.F );                 // (not there until it is its turn)
co_await draw( stage, straight, 0.8s );
co_await draw( stage, curved, 1.2s );

A curved arrow follows a Path, such as one from make_arc, and uses its first piece. An arrow too short for its head has none. arrow.set_drawn( fraction ) draws it as far as you like, for tying it to something else.

docs.title: Geometry
docs.text:
stage.visuals.add( make_polygon( theme, { a, b, c }, { .fill = Color{ palette.blue.r, palette.blue.g, palette.blue.b, 0.2F }, .labels = { "A", "B", "C" }, .dots = true } ) );
stage.visuals.add( make_angle( theme, b, a, c, { .radius = 0.5F } ) );
stage.visuals.add( make_angle( theme, a, b, c, { .radius = 1.2F, .color = palette.orange, .label = "θ" } ) );
stage.visuals.add( make_labeled_brace( theme, a, b, "adjacent", FontStyle{ Intent::LABEL }, { .color = palette.muted, .left = false } ) );

make_polygon takes the corners; fill, labels and dots are in PolygonOptions. make_angle marks the angle at a vertex between two points, as an arc (a right angle gets a little square, unless square_for_right is off).

docs.title: Morphing
docs.text:
A morph turns one visual into another: a circle into a square, a letter into a different letter, a formula into the next step of its derivation, a sentence into an edited sentence. Both visuals are flattened to outlines, their parts are paired up and cut to match, and the shape is blended from one to the other.

The code on this page is from the morphing and narration examples (examples/morphing, examples/narration), which are built with Voxima.

auto square = std::make_unique<Rectangle>( 0.6F, 0.6F, theme.palette().green );
square->position = circle.position;
co_await morph( stage, circle, std::move( square ), 1.5s, ease_cubic_in_out );

What happens to the visuals:

  • from must be a direct child of stage.visuals, or of the group given as MorphOptions::parent, with to made for that group's frame. It is taken off for the morph and dies with it: do not use its reference afterwards.
  • to takes its place when the morph finishes, so the last frame is the real thing, not a flattened copy. Keep a raw pointer to it before you move it in if you will animate it next:
Visual *next = square.get();
co_await morph( stage, *shown, std::move( square ), 1s, ease_cubic_in_out );
shown = next;

docs.title: How parts are matched
docs.text:
Each leaf (a glyph, a shape) of the two visuals is paired with one of the other. By default (LeafMatch::AUTO):

  1. words of laid-out text, kept in reading order;
  2. leaves with the same tag;
  3. identical glyphs, in reading order;
  4. what is left, by closeness (only leaves near each other and of similar size).

A leaf with no partner fades out or in. A pair that is the same shape only moved, turned or scaled (the head of an arrow that turns) is carried there whole.

So for a derivation, tag the parts that should be followed from one step to the next:

const Expr a = tag( "a", text( "a" ) );
const Expr b = tag( "b", text( "b" ) );
const Expr expanded = row(
    { ord( superscript( a, text( "2" ) ) ),
      bin( "+" ),
      ord( text( "2ab" ) ),
      bin( "+" ),
      ord( superscript( b, text( "2" ) ) ) } );

Here the a and b slide into place; everything else matches by glyph, and the parentheses fade.

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
MorphOptions options;
options.leaves = LeafMatch::BY_WORD;   // BY_WORD, BY_TAG, ... instead of AUTO
options.stagger = 0.4F;                // start the parts one after another (0 to 0.95 of the time)
options.part_ease = smooth;            // an ease for each part's own progress
co_await morph( stage, *shown, std::move( target ), 1.7s, ease_cubic_in_out, options );

stagger makes a word change letter by letter, left to right.

docs.title: Driving a morph yourself
docs.text:
morph_driven takes the thing that decides when: a scene that calls morph.set( t ) as it goes. That is how a morph is tied to narration:

co_await morph_driven(
    stage,
    *shown,
    std::move( square ),
    MorphOptions{},
    [&]( Morph &m ) { return narration.track_markers( "a", "b", [&m, smooth]( float t ) { m.set( smooth( t ) ); } ); } );

set( t ) blends from from (0) to to (1); values outside that overshoot, which is what back and elastic eases do. A picture (Image) is not an outline and cannot blend; see Visuals.

docs.title: Narration, subtitles and languages
docs.text:
A scene can be narrated: a text-to-speech model reads lines from the script in a chosen voice, in every language of the video, and the animation follows the speech. Subtitles for every language are made along with it.

The code on this page is from the narration example (examples/narration), which is built with Voxima.

docs.title: Voices
docs.text:
A narrator is a name in the script's voices section, pointing at a short reference clip; the speech is made in that voice.

voices::
  narrator: "chatterbox/en-voice-zero-robert-middleton.wav"

The path is relative to --tts-voice-dir (without it: voices, $VOXIMA_VOICES, or the installed <prefix>/share/voxima/voices, see Speech models and voices). A project with its own clips can keep them in a voices folder, but then the installed ones are not looked at: copy any of them it also uses. Give each language its own clip, in a voice of that language, in that language's file. Use clips you have the right to use, and credit them as their licenses ask for (a voice's source and license should be kept next to it).

The clips in Voxima's voices/chatterbox/ (installed in <prefix>/share/voxima/voices/chatterbox/) are all CC0 or public domain (LibriVox recordings, the Kyutai voice donations and Voice-Zero), so no credit is needed, though crediting the readers is kind. The source of each is in voices/chatterbox/SOURCES.md.

Chatterbox speaks many languages (English, French, German, Spanish and Polish among them). Chinese and Japanese text can be shown but cannot be narrated. Subtitle timing (the optional aligner model) is not available for every language either; a language without it still gets subtitles, timed by distributing the words along each line.

docs.title: Speaking in a scene
docs.text:
Scene intro( Stage &stage, Script &script )
{
    Narration narration;
    narration.setup( "narrator", script, stage.audio );     // the voice's name in the script
    narration.speech( "intro" );                            // the text: a path of keys into the script

    co_await choreograph(
        narration.play(),                                   // plays it through
        /* ...whatever else the scene animates, at the same time... */ wait_for( stage, 0.1s ) );
}
  • setup( name, script, stage.audio ) finds the voice for every language in use.
  • speech( keys... ) fetches the multi-line text under those keys in each language, makes the audio for all of them, and returns how long the longest takes. The speech is only made here; it is heard when play() runs.
  • play() is a scene: it runs for as long as the narration does. Run it alongside the animation with choreograph.

You can call speech() again after the previous one is finished, to say something else later in the same scene.

docs.title: Following the speech
docs.text:
Line breaks and markers in the script are the places to sync to, and they line up across languages.

Lines. Each line of the multi-line text starts a sync point:

auto second_line = [&]() -> Scene
{
    co_await narration.until_line( 1 );          // when the second line starts
    mark.color = theme.palette().green;
};

This is the robust choice: it is correct in every language and even when the shown text and the spoken text differ in length (<written|spoken>).

Markers. For finer points inside a line, write {name} in every language's text, then:

auto cues = [&]() -> Scene
{
    co_await narration.until_marker( "a" );
    co_await narration.track_markers( "a", "b", [&]( float t ) { dot.radius = 0.5F + t; } );   // t: 0 to 1 between the two
    co_await narration.track_to_end( "b", [&]( float t ) { dot.radius = 1.5F - t; } );
    double when = narration.marker_time( "a" );                  // seconds, in the first language's narration
    ( void ) when;
};

track_markers calls your function every frame with how far through the words between the markers the narration has got (and exactly 1 at the end): a morph tied to it lands on the words.

Words. until_word( i ), until_word_end( i ) and track_words( first, last, fn ) use word numbers of the first language only: words differ in number and length between languages, so use lines and markers when the video is in more than one.

until_time( seconds ) and track_time( from, to, fn ) use seconds since the batch started.

Sync by line or marker

Narration in another language takes a different time. Animations that wait on until_line and until_marker follow whatever each language takes; fixed wait_for times do not.

docs.title: Subtitles
docs.text: Subtitles are made for every narrated line, in every language, from the written text (<written|spoken> shows the written side). They are written as subtitles.<lang>.srt and .vtt in the render directory, and put in the video as one subtitle track per language. A subtitle that you want on the screen itself (a caption in the picture) is an ordinary visual: show the line when until_line( i ) is reached.

docs.title: Word effects
docs.text:
Light up each word as it is said (karaoke), pop it, underline it:

using namespace word_effects;
const Palette &palette = theme.palette();

const auto lines = script.fetch( lang, "intro" ).as_multiline();
StyledText styled( strip_markers( lines[0] ) );
styled.set_font_style( 0, styled.size(), FontStyle{ Intent::PROSE }.large() );
auto &text = stage.visuals.add( make_styled_text( theme, styled ) );
center_group( text );

auto words = narration.animate_words( text, all( { color( palette.muted, palette.yellow, stage.foreground ), pop( 1.15F ) } ) );

Ready-made effects: reveal() (invisible until said, then fades in), color( before, during, after ), pop( scale ), underline( color ); all( { ... } ) combines them. The colors are blended, so give the colors the word is seen in: for the text color use stage.foreground, not white. For several lines, pass first_word (the number of the line's first word in the narration).

You can write your own effect: it is a coroutine receiving a WordContext (the word, its times, the clock):

Scene wiggle( WordContext word )
{
    co_await word.over_word( [&]( float t ) { word.word.rotation = 0.1F * std::sin( 20.F * t ); } );
    word.word.rotation = 0.F;
}

narration.on_words( text, callback ) is the simpler form: call a function as each word starts.

docs.title: Several languages
docs.text:
voxima ... --lang en --lang fr              # one video: an audio and a subtitle track for each language
voxima ... --lang en --lang fr --separate   # one video per language, in <render-dir>/en/ and <render-dir>/fr/
  • Together (the default): one video, timed to the first language (the master), with a track for each language. The languages are kept in step: narration is divided at its markers and at each line start, and every segment is given the time the slowest language takes, so a marker falls at the same moment in every language's audio. The faster languages get silence at the end of a segment: nobody is cut off. --max-speedup 1.15 lets the others be speeded up by up to 15% (needs ffmpeg) so there is less silence; the master is never speeded up. A language whose markers or lines do not match the master's cannot be kept in step: it is warned about and left as it is.
  • --separate: each language is a complete render of its own, with its text on screen and its animation timed to its own narration, so scenes must follow the narration (until_line, until_marker) rather than fixed times. The models are loaded once for all of them.

docs.title: Your own plugin project
docs.text: Scenes live in a plugin: a shared library (.so on Linux and macOS, .dll on Windows) that voxima loads with --plugin. A plugin project is a small CMake project built against your Voxima build, installed with make install PREFIX=<prefix> (see Installing). A starting point is in <prefix>/share/voxima/examples (or examples/ in the checkout), one folder per example.

docs.title: The CMake project
docs.text:
cmake_minimum_required( VERSION 3.31 )
project( MyVideo CXX )

find_package( Voxima REQUIRED )

voxima_add_plugin( myvideo scenes.cpp more_scenes.cpp )

voxima_add_plugin( name sources... ) makes a module called name, links it to Voxima's core, turns on C++20 and coroutines, and names it name.so or name.dll. Exactly one of its source files must contain VOXIMA_PLUGIN();.

find_package( Voxima ) finds the Voxima you installed, and the plugin is built against its headers. A plugin is only good for that Voxima: one loaded by a voxima of another version is refused (see below). To insist on a version, write it (find_package( Voxima 0.1.0 REQUIRED )); only that exact version matches.

Configure with the install folder as the prefix path. The install is all a plugin needs:

cmake -S . -B build -G Ninja -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release -DCMAKE_PREFIX_PATH=<prefix>
cmake --build build

docs.title: Building just as the program was
docs.text:
Scenes share the program's strings, functions and coroutines, so a plugin must be built with:

  • the same compiler and version,
  • the same standard library,
  • the same Debug or Release configuration (make install installs the Release build),
  • the same Voxima version.

Each plugin records what it was built with. One that does not match is refused when loaded, naming both, rather than crashing in some distant way. On Linux a plugin should be built with the system's default libstdc++ ABI.

docs.title: Several plugins
docs.text:
--plugin can be given more than once, and scene names from all of them are one list. --plugin-dir <folder> loads every plugin (.so or .dll) in a folder, in name order, so a folder of plugins is one command:

voxima --plugin-dir build/plugins --list-scenes

A file in the folder that cannot be loaded (built with another compiler, or not a plugin) is skipped with a warning, rather than stopping the rest; with --plugin, it is an error. Keep plugins in a folder of their own, since the core library is a .so too. A scene in one plugin can play a scene from another by name. If two plugins register the same name, the one loaded later takes it, so keep names distinct.

docs.title: Working fast
docs.text: Use --preview and keep the window open while you build: the plugin is loaded again when it is rebuilt, and the scene you were watching starts again with your change. See Rendering.

docs.title: Debugging
docs.text: Build with -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Debug against a Debug build of Voxima (make debug makes it; install it with cmake --install build/Debug --prefix <dir> --component Voxima, with its own <dir>). A scene that throws shows the message in the preview window's title and on stderr.

docs.title: If the plugin is refused
docs.text: A plugin built with a different compiler, standard library, configuration or Voxima version is refused when it is loaded. The message names what the plugin was built with and what the program was built with. Rebuild the plugin with the compiler and configuration Voxima was built with.

docs.title: Render a video
docs.text:
voxima --plugin build/hello --script-dir scripts --lang en --theme "Academic Classic" \
       --render-dir render --container mkv --vcodec h264 --acodec opus
Option --plugin A plugin of scenes (repeatable; the .so / .dll extension may be left out) --scene A scene to render; repeat to play several in order (default: the one called movie) --lang A language; repeat for several (the first is the master). See Narration --script-dir Where <lang>.huml files are --theme, --theme-dir, --palette Look: see Themes --width, --height, --fps Picture size and frame rate (1280×720 at 24 fps by default) --container mp4, mkv or webm --vcodec h264, h265, vp9 or av1 --acodec flac, wav, aac, opus or vorbis --render-dir Where the output goes --font-dir Fonts (see Installing)

Every option is in the command line reference.

Not every container takes every codec; if a combination is refused, try another (mkv takes nearly all of them).

docs.title: What is in the render directory
docs.text:
• final.<container>: the video, with an audio and a subtitle track for every language.
  • subtitles.<lang>.srt and subtitles.<lang>.vtt: the subtitles, for each language, to use on their own (YouTube takes .srt or .vtt).
  • The pieces it was made from, such as each language's audio, and the tts-cache folder (see below).

With --separate, each language is in its own folder, <render-dir>/<lang>/, with its own final.<container>.

--save-svg and --save-png also keep every frame as an SVG or PNG file (a lot of files; handy for stills).

Speech is cached in a tts-cache folder inside the render directory, so rendering again after a change to the animation (not the words) does not have to make the speech again. Keep that folder between renders.

docs.title: Choose scenes
docs.text:
voxima --plugin build/hello --list-scenes                  # what the plugin has
voxima --plugin build/hello ... --scene intro              # one scene
voxima --plugin build/hello ... --scene intro --scene end  # several, in order

An unknown scene name is reported (with the list) before any model or font is loaded.

docs.title: Preview
docs.text:
voxima --plugin build/hello --script-dir scripts --lang en --theme "Academic Classic" --preview

--preview plays the video in a window with sound, instead of rendering a file (the first language only). It runs at your display's refresh rate. Controls:

Key Space Pause and resume L, K, J Play forwards, pause, play backwards Left, Right Step one frame back or forward (paused) Home, End Go to the start or the end [ and ] The previous and the next scene Up, Down Skip a second forward or back R Repeat the scene being watched F5 Reload the plugin and the script Esc Close

Live editing: a rebuilt plugin is loaded again by itself. The scenes start again with the new code, and the window goes back to where it was in the scene being watched. If the new build cannot be loaded, or a scene fails, the problem is shown in the window's title and on stderr, and the next build is tried when it comes. (What is loaded is a copy of the plugin, so the build can write over the file.) F5 also reloads the script, so you can edit the words too.

docs.title: Missing glyphs
docs.text:
A character that cannot be drawn is never left to fail quietly. Two things count:

  • a character no real font in the theme has (the catch-all NotDef font at the end of every stack draws a box for anything, so it does not count), and
  • U+FFFD, the replacement character, which is what a missing script value or badly encoded text turns into.

Each is drawn as a magenta box with the character's code in it, keeping the text's spacing. When the render finishes, every one is listed with the text it was in:

WARNING: 2 missing glyphs (drawn as magenta boxes in the video):
  U+FFFD  in "A script value that is missing: ..."
  U+10FFFD  in "A character no font has: ..."

--strict-glyphs makes the render exit with an error if there were any, which is what you want in an automated build. Text that is not valid UTF-8 is rejected outright.

docs.title: Music and sound effects
docs.text:
The code on this page is from the sound example (examples/sound), which is built with Voxima.

Any sound file (WAV, FLAC, Ogg, MP3) can be played into the video with stage.audio.play. It starts at the frame being made, and carries on by itself, across scenes, until its end or until you stop it. It is mixed into every language's audio track. Any number play at once.

Sound music;
if ( const char *file = std::getenv( "VOXIMA_MUSIC" ); file != nullptr && std::filesystem::exists( file ) )
{
    music = stage.audio.play( file, { .volume = -22.0, .loop = true, .fade_in = 2s } );
}
else
{
    std::cerr << "No music: set VOXIMA_MUSIC to a sound file to have some\n";
}
music.fade_out( 2s );

SoundOptions:

Option Meaning volume In dB: 0 is as recorded, -6 about half as loud loop Start again at the end, until stopped or faded out fade_in Rise from silence to the volume over this long from Start this far into the sound

play returns a Sound, to change it later: set_volume( db, over ), fade_out( over ), stop(). The sound plays on whether or not you keep it, so you only need it if you will change it. A file is read once however often it is played. stage.audio.stop_sounds() stops everything at once.

Volume changes are smooth ramps, so they do not click.

docs.title: Sounds made in code
docs.text:
play also takes an AudioBuffer of samples your program made (any rate and channel count; it is made stereo at the track's rate). The sound example (examples/sound) makes a plucked note this way:

// A plucked note, made rather than read from a file: a sine that dies away over `seconds`
AudioBuffer pluck( float frequency, float seconds = 2.F )
{
    constexpr size_t rate = 48000;
    AudioBuffer note( static_cast<size_t>( seconds * rate ), rate, 1 );
    for ( size_t f = 0; f < note.frames(); ++f )
    {
        const float t = static_cast<float>( f ) / rate;
        const float attack = std::min( 1.F, t / 0.005F ); // no click at the start
        note.frame( f )[0] = attack * std::exp( -3.F * t / seconds * 2.F ) * std::sin( 2.F * 3.14159265F * frequency * t );
    }
    return note;
}

docs.title: Tying a sound to an animation
docs.text:
Play the sound at the moment the animation does something, in the same scene:

// The sound starts at the frame being made, so with the animation
stage.audio.play( pluck( notes[i] ), { .volume = -14.0 } );
co_await grow_in( stage, dot, 0.5s );

Narration is separate (it has its own voice and sync; see Narration); music and effects are mixed with it.

docs.title: Text and math
docs.text:
Text is laid out with real shaping (HarfBuzz) and bidirectional reordering, so it works for any script the fonts have: Latin, Cyrillic, Greek, Arabic, Hebrew, Chinese, Japanese and more, mixed in one line if you like. The result is vector outlines like any other visual: you can move, scale, fade or morph it.

The code on this page is from the text-math example (examples/text-math), which is built with Voxima.

docs.title: One piece of text
docs.text:
auto &title = stage.visuals.add( make_text( theme, "Hello, Voxima", FontStyle{ Intent::TITLE }.large(), "en" ) );
move_to( title, { 0.F, 3.F }, Anchor::TOP );

make_text( theme, string, style, language ). The text's baseline is at y = 0 and it is not centered: its origin is the left end of the first baseline. Use center_group( *text ) to put the middle of it on the origin, or move_to to place it.

Give the language (a BCP-47 tag like "fr" or "zh-Hans") so the shaper picks the right glyph forms. When the text came from the script, use the script's language. Line breaks in the string make several lines (TextLayout sets the align and line_spacing).

Paragraphs wrap to a width, at spaces:

auto &para = stage.visuals.add( make_paragraph( theme, long_text, FontStyle{ Intent::PROSE }, 10.F, lang,
    TextLayout{ .align = TextAlign::CENTER } ) );

(Only for languages that put spaces between words.)

docs.title: Font styles
docs.text:
A FontStyle says what the text is for (its intent) and how it should look; the theme decides which actual font that is. So a scene works with any theme.

const FontStyle for_a_title{ Intent::TITLE };                       // what it is for
const FontStyle chained = FontStyle{ Intent::PROSE }.large().bold();  // chained changes
const FontStyle small_code = FontStyle{ Intent::CODE }.small();
Intents PROSE, TITLE, LABEL, ANNOTATION, CAPTION Text of different roles CODE Monospace MATH The math font

Chain: .tiny() .small() .medium() .large() .huge() for size; .light() .regular() .bold() .black() for weight; .upright() .italic() .oblique() .math_italic() for slant; .sans() .serif() .slab() .mono() .script() .fraktur() .double_struck() for the kind of letter. Text sizes do not vary between themes: a theme is which fonts, not how big. If a font has no glyph for a character, the next font in the theme's stack is tried.

docs.title: Styled text: several looks in one piece
docs.text:
Build a StyledText and set styles on ranges of characters:

StyledText text( "Hello\nالعالم" );
text.set_font_style( 0, text.size(), FontStyle{ Intent::TITLE }.large() );
text.set_color( 0, 5, stage.theme->palette().red );
text.set_weight( 2, 4, Weight::BLACK );

auto &label = stage.visuals.add( make_styled_text( *stage.theme, text ) );
center_group( label );

Ranges are ( start, end ) over the text; there are setters for color, weight, slant, scale, width, kind, intent and language. Words come out as groups tagged word0, word1, ... (that is how word effects work).

docs.title: Formulas
docs.text:
Formulas are built from small functions that describe them, and laid out only when you build them, each part in its own size: numerators, subscripts and radicands come out right on their own.

using namespace math;
using namespace math::literals;

Context context( theme );          // the theme and the body size; large by default

auto formula = eq( "a"_m * "a"_m + "b"_m * "b"_m, "c"_m * "c"_m );     // aa + bb = cc
auto &shown = stage.visuals.add( formula.build( context ) );

A formula is an Expr: cheap to copy, and can be built any number of times (build( context, MathStyle::text() ) for in-line size).

Operators read like the math: a + b, a - b, -a, a * b (side by side, no sign; times( a, b ) for ×), a / b (a fraction), eq lt gt leq geq neq, and "x"_m (math italic) and "sin"_u (upright). The spacing is the spacing TeX uses.

Building blocks (math/Expr.h):

Text text (math italic), upright, bold, words (for "if", "for all"), script, fraktur, double_struck, sans, mono Shapes fraction, binomial, radical, root, superscript, subscript, scripts, primed, overset, underset, substack, continued_fraction Big operators sum, product, integral, large_operator; limits lim max min sup inf gcd; functions sin cos tan log ln exp ... Fences parens, brackets, braces, bars, fenced( open, content, close ), big Marks overline, underline, overbrace, underbrace, hat, tilde, bar, dot, vec, widehat, ... Grids matrix, pmatrix, bmatrix, vmatrix, cases, aligned (equations lined up as TeX's align) Rows row( { ord( ... ), bin( "+" ), rel( "=" ), ... } ): atoms of a class, spaced as TeX does Symbols sym::alpha, sym::leq, sym::infty, sym::Rightarrow, ... (Greek, relations, operators, arrows)

A fuller formula:

auto quadratic = row( {
    ord( "x" ), rel( "=" ),
    ord( fraction(
        row( { ord( "−b" ), bin( sym::pm ), ord( radical( row( { ord( superscript( text( "b" ), text( "2" ) ) ),
                                                                  bin( "−" ), ord( "4ac" ) } ) ) ) } ),
        text( "2a" ) ) ) } );

Marking parts: colored( color, part ), cancel( part ) (a strike through, for terms that cancel), boxed( part ), and tag( "name", part ) to find a part again after the build (to animate it):

auto halved = eq( "x"_m, fraction( tag( "half", text( "a" ) ), text( "2" ) ) );
auto &tagged = stage.visuals.add( halved.build( context ) );
Visual *half = find_tag( tagged, "half" );

Greek letters set by text() are italic, as in TeX; capitals are upright (upright( sym::Gamma )). See math/Symbols.h for the names. words( "if" ) is for words between formulas.

docs.title: Code listings
docs.text:
auto listing = make_code( *stage.theme, code::Language::CPP, R"cpp(

// The sum of the squares, the long way
template<typename T>
T sum_of_squares( const std::vector<T> &values )
{
    constexpr int START = 0;
    T total = START;
    for ( const T &v: values )
    {
        total += v * v; // no overflow check
    }
    return total;
}
)cpp" );
    center_group( *listing );
    auto &shown = stage.visuals.add( std::move( listing ) );

C and C++ are highlighted with the theme's code colors. Two helpers animate a listing:

Typewriter typer( shown );
co_await typer.type( stage );
co_await wait_for( stage, 1s );

// Then pointed out, as narration would: a line, a range of lines, and two separate places, and away again
LineHighlight pointer( shown, *stage.theme );
co_await pointer.to( stage, Lines( 5 ), 0.4s );                        // the signature
co_await wait_for( stage, 1.5s );
co_await pointer.to( stage, Lines( 9, 12 ), 0.5s );                    // the loop
co_await wait_for( stage, 1.5s );
co_await pointer.to( stage, Lines{ { 7, 8 }, { 13, 13 } }, 0.5s );     // where it starts, and what it gives back
co_await wait_for( stage, 1.5s );
co_await pointer.to( stage, Lines(), 0.4s );

Lines are numbered from 1, as an editor numbers them. Lines outside the listing are ignored.

docs.title: Themes
docs.text: A theme is the look of a video: which fonts text is set in, and the colors it starts with. Choose a built-in one with --theme "Academic Classic" (names below), or write your own (see Theme files). Without --theme, a theme.huml next to the scripts is used, or else Modern Technical. Colors can be changed apart from the fonts with --palette, so any palette goes with any theme.

docs.title: Modern Technical
docs.text:
This is a clean, highly legible theme designed for explaining software engineering or modern physics. It pairs well with the crispness of CJK Gothic fonts.

  • Main Font: FiraGO (High x-height, humanist, excellent legibility).
  • Math Font: NewCM Math (The standard for modern, clean LaTeX-style rendering).
  • Emoji Font: Noto Emoji (Variable) (Blobs/Outlines that match Fira’s stroke weight).
  • CJK Fallback: Noto Sans CJK (Clean, modern, and weight-accurate).
  • Monospace Fallback: Fira Mono.
  • Code: Fira Mono, in the colors of GitHub's dark theme (Fira Mono has no italic, so comments are only a color).

docs.title: Academic Classic
docs.text:
This theme mimics the look of a prestigious textbook or a formal research paper. It’s perfect for pure mathematics or historical topics.

  • Main Font: New Computer Modern (Book/Regular) (The gold standard for academic "TeX" looks).
  • Math Font: NewCM Math (Native pairing with the text font).
  • Emoji Font: Symbola (More literal, detailed illustrations that fit a "printed" look).
  • CJK Fallback: Source Han Serif (A "Mincho" style that matches the serifs of NewCM).
  • Monospace Fallback: New Computer Modern Mono.
  • Code: New Computer Modern Mono, like a printed textbook's listing: warm, muted inks, bold keywords, italic comments.

docs.title: Engineering Blueprint
docs.text:
A high-contrast, technical theme that feels like an architectural drawing or an IDE. It emphasizes structure and geometry.

  • Main Font: IBM Plex Sans (Engineered, rigid, but human-friendly).
  • Math Font: STIX Two Math (A sharp, technical math font often used in scientific publishing).
  • Emoji Font: Noto Emoji (Variable) (Keep it minimal to avoid distracting from the technical data).
  • CJK Fallback: IBM Plex Sans CJK (Specifically designed to sit alongside Plex Latin).
  • Monospace Fallback: IBM Plex Mono.
  • Code: IBM Plex Mono, like a blueprint: cyan and white, amber for literals, bold function names, italic comments.

docs.title: Playful Discovery
docs.text:
A softer, more approachable theme for educational content aimed at a general audience or younger students.

  • Main Font: Comfortaa or Quicksand (Rounded, friendly, and very "bouncy" for animations).
  • Math Font: GFS Neohellenic Math (A rounded, sans-serif math font that is rare but very friendly).
  • Emoji Font: Noto Emoji (Variable) (Perfect for this "soft" aesthetic).
  • CJK Fallback: Kosugi Maru (A Japanese rounded Gothic that matches the main font's soft terminals).
  • Code: DejaVu Sans Mono, in soft pastels (the colors of Catppuccin Mocha), italic comments.

docs.title: New Computer Modern
docs.text: • Code: New Computer Modern Mono, in the colors of One Dark (CodePalette::dark), italic comments.

docs.title: Palettes
docs.text:
A theme is fonts; the colors are a Palette, chosen apart from it: any palette works with any theme. Each theme starts with one of its own, whole - background and text included - and --palette name (or theme.set_palette( Palette::get( name ) ) and stage.use_palette( theme.palette() ) in a scene) changes it to another. A theme with no palette of its own starts on plain black (Palette::house( "one-dark" ), Theme's own default) instead.

A palette names roles, not uses: background, text, muted (axes, grids, comments), and eight accents (red orange yellow green cyan blue purple pink). Code colors (palette.code), a plot's curve colors (the accents in turn: blue, orange, green ...) and the band behind pointed-out lines all come from them, so they suit the background whichever it is.

  • Dark: one-dark, github-dark, catppuccin-mocha, academic, blueprint (the themes' own, in that order of theme: New Computer Modern, Modern Technical, Playful Discovery, Academic Classic, Engineering Blueprint).
  • Light: github-light, catppuccin-latte, solarized-light, paper.
  • Your own: Palette::add( palette ), then by name.

Text, axes and lines are drawn in the palette's text color where nothing else was chosen: pure white means "the theme's text color" (Color::resolved, Stage::foreground), so a scene written for a dark background reads on a light one. Anything given a color of its own keeps it: use the palette's accents for those (stage.theme->palette().blue), not fixed RGB, if the scene should work on both.

docs.title: Theme files
docs.text:
A theme is a HUML file (themes/*.huml for the built-in ones, which are compiled in): the fonts as named families put in stacks, and the palette it starts with. Your own can start from a built-in one, or from another file, and change only what it likes:

meta::
  name: "My Course"
  inherit: "Modern Technical"     # a built-in theme, or <name>.huml in a --theme-dir (or next to the scripts)

palette: "github-light"           # the colors it starts with, whole (see Palettes; --palette changes it)
                                  # or the colors themselves, see below

fonts::                           # families: what a style becomes a file through
  plex_mono::
    regular: "IBMPlexMono-Regular.ttf"
    italic: "IBMPlexMono-Italic.ttf"
    bold: "IBMPlexMono-Bold.ttf"

stacks::                          # lists of families: what the first has no glyph for, the next may
  code:: "plex_mono", "...fallbacks"        # "...name" puts in another stack's families

intents::                         # which stack each kind of text uses
  code: "code"

A theme file can hold its own colors instead of naming a palette, so a project's theme file is all it needs for its look, with no Palette::add or use_palette in the scenes:

palette::
  inherit: "one-dark"             # optional: the colors it does not give
  name: "my-colors"               # optional: the theme's name otherwise
  background: "#101820"
  blue: "#4FB3FF"

Colors are "#RRGGBB": background, text, muted, and the accents red orange yellow green cyan blue purple pink. Without inherit it has to give all eleven. A palette added with Palette::add in a plugin is not there yet when the theme file is read, so inherit names a built-in palette. The code's colors are worked out from the accents again (see derive_code_palette), and two theme files that inherit one another merge their palette:: key by key. --palette still replaces it all.

Use it with --theme my-course.huml (or --theme my-course with --theme-dir pointing at it), or call it theme.huml in the script directory and it is used when no --theme is given.

Families are one of four forms (see FontFamily.h):

  • files, by weight and slant: light regular bold black and their _italic (italic is regular's); an optional small:: with the same keys for the tiny and small sizes (an optical size drawn for small text). A style with no file is the nearest that has one: the same slant with the weight moved toward regular (black to bold to regular, light to regular), then the upright. So a family with only regular and bold serves black, light and any italic.
  • variable: "file": a variable font, its weight, width and slant axes set by the style (or fixed with weight, width, slant).
  • collection: "file" with faces:: light: 5, regular: 10, ...: a font collection, a face for each weight.
  • notdef: "file": the catch-all font that ends a stack, drawing a box for every character.

Overriding is by merging. A dict (a family, fonts, intents) is merged key by key, so fonts:: fira:: bold: "..." changes only that file; a stack (or anything else) given again replaces what it inherits. A mistake in a file (an unknown key, a family that is not there, a stack that contains itself) is an error that says which file, and what.

The intents are prose, code, title, label, annotation, caption and math. Text size does not vary between themes (ThemeUtils::get_theme_font_size): a theme is which files, not how big.

The built-in files are the record of what fonts each theme uses, and a test (tests/data/font_stacks.txt, made by UPDATE_GOLDEN=1) keeps them to it: every intent, weight, slant and size loads the same files as before.

docs.title: Visuals and layout
docs.text: The code on this page is from the layout example (examples/layout), which is built with Voxima.

docs.title: Shapes
docs.text:
auto circle = std::make_unique<Circle>( 0.7F, theme.palette().blue );   // radius, color
auto &dot = stage.visuals.add( std::move( circle ) );
dot.position = { -3.F, 0.F };

auto &box = stage.visuals.add( std::make_unique<Rectangle>( 1.F, 0.5F, theme.palette().green ) );  // half width, half height

Every visual has the same properties:

Property Meaning position Where its origin is, in its parent's frame (stage units, y up) rotation, scale_x, scale_y Turned and scaled about its origin color Fill color (alpha makes it see-through) fill_gradient A fill that changes color across it, instead (see Gradients) opacity How see-through it is as a whole, 0 to 1: unlike the colors' alpha, what overlaps inside a group does not show through stroke_thickness, stroke_color, stroke_dash Its outline (see Dashed lines) tags Names for finding it again (see Tags)

Line has a start and end; a Path is made of MoveTo and CubicTo commands; Group holds other visuals. A group's position, rotation, scale and color multiply down into its children, so fading a group fades everything in it.

docs.title: Groups
docs.text:
auto &row = stage.visuals.add( std::make_unique<Group>() );
row.add( std::make_unique<Circle>( 0.4F ) );
row.add( std::make_unique<Circle>( 0.4F ) );

Iterate a group with a range-for; size(), clear(), remove( &child ) (hands the child back) and replace( &old, new ) work on its direct children.

docs.title: Drawing order
docs.text:
A group draws its children in order, so what comes later is in front. To put something elsewhere in that order, use insert( index, visual ) (0 is the back) instead of add, or move a child that is already there:

stage.visuals.to_front( &back );                                            // now the rectangle hides the circle
auto &behind = stage.visuals.insert( 0, std::make_unique<Circle>( 2.F, palette.green ) ); // behind them both

to_front, to_back, raise and lower take a direct child, and return false if it is not one. All of these stay in front of the stage's background.

docs.title: Dashed lines
docs.text:
Any stroke can be dashed or dotted, with a StrokeDash:

auto &line = stage.visuals.add( std::make_unique<Line>() );
line.stroke_color = palette.blue;
line.start = { -5.F, 2.F };
line.end = { 5.F, 2.F };
line.stroke_thickness = 0.06F;
line.stroke_dash = StrokeDash::dashed( 0.4F, 0.2F ); // 0.4 on, 0.2 off

auto &ring = stage.visuals.add( std::make_unique<Circle>( 1.2F, Color{ 1.F, 1.F, 1.F, 0.F } ) );
ring.stroke_color = palette.orange;
ring.stroke_thickness = 0.12F;
ring.stroke_dash = StrokeDash::dotted( 0.3F );       // round dots, 0.3 apart

co_await tween( stage, 3s, ease_linear, [&]( float t ) { ring.stroke_dash.offset = -3.F * t; } ); // they march

A pattern is lengths on and off in turn, in the visual's own units, so it scales with the visual just as its stroke does (and stretches with it under an uneven scale). offset starts it further along; tween it for dashes that march. Each piece of a path (each MoveTo) starts the pattern again. A pattern under half a pixel is drawn as a whole line.

ConnectorOptions::dash dashes a connector's line and not its arrow heads, and GraphOptions::dash a graph's curve. Dashes stay as they are in draw_on, and a morph blends them: between two patterns, or with the gaps opening from a whole line. The exception is a line that becomes a filled shape: it is drawn as a whole line on the way, so the gaps close as soon as it starts.

docs.title: Gradients
docs.text:
Any shape can be filled with a linear or radial gradient instead of a plain color:

auto &bar = stage.visuals.add( std::make_unique<Rectangle>( 1.F, 2.F ) );
bar.fill_gradient = Gradient::across( box_of( bar ), 90.F, { { 0.F, Color::hex( 0x101010 ) }, { 1.F, Color::hex( 0xF0F0F0 ) } } );

auto &disc = stage.visuals.add( std::make_unique<Circle>( 2.F ) );
disc.fill_gradient = Gradient::radial( { 0.F, 0.F }, 2.F, { 0.7F, 0.7F }, { { 0.F, palette.yellow }, { 1.F, palette.red } } );

auto &title = stage.visuals.add( make_text( theme, "Gradients", FontStyle{ Intent::TITLE } ) );
fill_each_with_gradient( title, 90.F, { { 0.F, palette.blue }, { 1.F, palette.pink } } ); // a gradient per glyph

A gradient is placed in the visual's own coordinates, so it moves, turns and scales with the visual. Gradient::across fits a linear one to a box at an angle (0 goes to the right, 90 up); box_of gives that box only while the visual is still at its origin, so use it before placing the visual. Stops are at offsets from 0 to 1. The visual's color tints the gradient and its alpha fades it, and white in a stop is the theme's text color, as everywhere.

Text has a gradient per glyph, not one across a word: fill_each_with_gradient gives each shape below a visual its own, across that shape.

Colors blend as they are written, in sRGB and not in linear light; add stops to follow any other curve. A frame has 8 bits a channel and gradients are not dithered, so a long, dark ramp shows bands (from 0 to 16 across 1600 pixels: 17 bands, each about 94 pixels wide). Between stops with different alpha, Voxima's renderer blends colors premultiplied, so a color fading out does not pick up the hue of the transparent stop, as it would in a browser looking at the same SVG. A gradient that goes nowhere (its ends the same, or a radius of 0) is drawn in its last color.

A morph blends gradients: a plain fill and a gradient turn into one another, and two of a kind blend their stops and their places. A linear and a radial one cannot become one another, so they pass through a plain color, the average of the two:

auto square = std::make_unique<Rectangle>( 2.F, 2.F );
square->position = { 4.F, -0.5F };
square->fill_gradient = Gradient::across( AABB{ { -2.F, -2.F }, { 2.F, 2.F } }, 0.F, { { 0.F, palette.green }, { 1.F, palette.blue } } );
co_await morph( stage, disc, std::move( square ), 2s, ease_cubic_in_out ); // a radial one and a linear one pass through a plain color

docs.title: Placing things against each other
docs.text:
Hard-coded coordinates are fine for a couple of things. For anything more, place visuals relative to each other (visuals/Placement.h), so a change in size or text does not make things overlap. The boxes used are the ones layout uses: for text, the advance widths and line height, not just the ink.

move_to( title, { 0.F, 3.5F }, Anchor::TOP );          // its top edge at y = 3.5
next_to( label, dot, Anchor::BOTTOM );                 // under it, a gap between
next_to( panel, other, Anchor::RIGHT, 1.0F );          // to its right, 1 unit apart

Anchor is CENTER, LEFT, RIGHT, TOP, BOTTOM or a corner (TOP_LEFT, ...). Visuals placed against each other must be in the same group (or both directly on the stage).

Rows, columns and grids arrange the children of a group:

arrange_row( group, { .gap = 0.5F } );                     // left to right, centered on the origin
arrange_column( group, { .gap = 0.3F, .align = Align::START } );
arrange_grid( group, 3, { .column_gap = 0.4F, .row_gap = 0.2F } );   // rows of 3
distribute_row( group );                                   // equal spaces between, outer two stay put
align_edges( group, Anchor::LEFT );                        // line up on an edge

Align (across the direction of the row) is START, CENTER, END, or BASELINE, which lines up the baselines of text of any size.

Keeping things on screen:

keep_inside( group, safe_area( stage.camera ) );   // moved the least it takes
fit_inside( group, safe_area( stage.camera ) );    // and scaled down if it is too big

safe_area is the picture's frame, at zoom 1, pulled in by a margin (0.5 units by default).

box_of( visual ) and point_at( visual, anchor ) give a visual's box and one of its points, in its parent's frame, for your own placement.

docs.title: Frames and arcs
docs.text:
make_surround( visual, options ) makes a rectangle round a visual's box, without holding it as a panel does, and make_arc( center, radius, from_degrees, to_degrees, options ) part of a circle as a stroked Path:

auto &frame = stage.visuals.add( make_surround( word, { .radius = 0.1F, .outline = palette.yellow } ) );
auto &arc = stage.visuals.add( make_arc( { 3.F, -1.5F }, 1.F, 0.F, 270.F, { .thickness = 0.08F, .color = palette.green } ) );

Add a frame to the group its visual is in. It stays where it is if the visual moves.

docs.title: Panels, lists and tables
docs.text:
A panel is a rounded box fitted round something:

auto &panel = stage.visuals.add( make_panel( make_text( theme, "Theorem", style ), { .padding = 0.5F } ) );

PanelOptions sets the padding, corner radius, fill, outline and outline_width, and an optional shadow. The default fill and outline are faint tints of the text color, so a panel suits any palette.

A list is a bulleted or numbered column:

auto &list = stage.visuals.add( make_list( theme, { "first", "second", "third" }, { .numbered = true } ) );
list.row( 1 );    // each row is a visual of its own, to show or light on its own

Long items wrap if you set max_width; every row is spaced evenly.

A table has rows of cells, a header, and optional rules, stripes and wrapping:

const std::vector<std::vector<std::string>> rows = {
    { "Name", "Scale", "Use" },
    { "tiny", "0.5", "footnotes" },
    { "huge", "2.0", "titles" } };
auto &table = stage.visuals.add( make_table( theme, rows, { .striped = true, .max_width = 10.F } ) );
table.cell( 1, 2 );   // a cell is a visual

Cells can also be visuals (a formula, a picture); then give make_table a vector of rows of std::unique_ptr<Visual>.

docs.title: Pictures
docs.text: An Image shows a picture file: set its path, half_width and half_height. A picture is not an outline, so it morphs only into the same picture (moving to where that is); otherwise it cross-fades.

docs.title: Tags
docs.text:
Tag a visual to find it again after it is built into something bigger:

tag_visual( dot, "hero" );
Visual *found = find_tag( stage.visuals, "hero" );

A path of names looks inside each match in turn (find_tag( built, "fraction1", "bar" )). Math formulas and other composites name their own parts too (numerator, denominator, bar, ...), listed in visuals/Tags.h. Tags are also what morphing uses to follow a part from one visual to the next.
